subject: physics
title: Charge, current and drift velocity
key_idea: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, and charge always comes in whole multiples of the elementary charge e. In a conductor the carriers drift slowly, and the current is I = nAvq. The number density n explains why conductors, semiconductors and insulators behave so differently.

blocks.text: A current is a flow of charge carriers. This section defines current and charge and the units that go with them.

items.meaning: A particle that carries charge through a material.
The rate of flow of charge past a point.
The unit of charge. One coulomb passes a point each second when the current is one ampere.
The size of the charge on a proton or an electron: e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

blocks.label: Charge flowed in a steady current

diagram.question: A current of {I} mA flows in a wire for {t} minutes. Calculate the charge that flows past a point in the wire.

items: In **metals** the carriers are free electrons.
In **electrolytes** (solutions and molten ionic compounds) the carriers are positive and negative ions.
Electrons carry charge −e and protons carry charge +e.
**Conventional current** is drawn from the positive terminal of a source round to the negative terminal.
**Electron flow** is the real movement of electrons in a metal. It is the opposite way, from negative to positive.
In an electrolyte, positive ions move with the conventional current and negative ions move against it.
I = ΔQ / Δt, so one ampere is one coulomb per second.
Q = It for a steady current.
Conventional current runs from + to −, opposite to electron flow.

blocks.text: Charge is not continuous. The charge on any particle or object is a whole-number multiple of the elementary charge e.

blocks.label: Quantised charge
where: Q = net charge on a particle or object (C)
N = a whole number, positive or negative

items: A charge of 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is not possible, because it is 1.5 times e.
An object that has lost three electrons has a net charge of +3e.
Every charge is a whole-number multiple of e.
Electron: −e. Proton: +e.

blocks.text: Free electrons in a metal move quickly and randomly. When a potential difference is applied, they also drift slowly along the wire.

items.meaning: The average velocity of the charge carriers along the conductor, caused by the electric field.
The number of charge carriers per unit volume (m⁻³).

blocks.label: Current in a conductor
where: n = number density of charge carriers (m⁻³)
q = charge on each carrier (C), which is e for electrons

items.text: In a time Δt the carriers move a distance vΔt, so a volume A v Δt of the wire passes a point.
That volume holds n A v Δt carriers.
Each carries charge q, so ΔQ = n A v Δt q.
Divide by Δt: I = ΔQ / Δt = n A v q.

diagram.alt: Change the current, the cross-sectional area and the metal to see the electron drift velocity.

items: Drift velocity is tiny, often a fraction of a millimetre per second, yet a lamp lights at once because every electron in the circuit starts to drift together.
For the same current, a thinner wire (smaller A) needs a larger drift velocity.
For the same current and area, a material with a smaller n needs a larger drift velocity.
I = nAvq, with q = e for electrons.
Drift velocity is small; the random speed of the electrons is much greater.
Fewer carriers or a thinner wire means a larger drift velocity for the same current.

blocks.text: The three kinds of material differ mainly in n, the number density of charge carriers.

rows: Very large, about 10²⁸ m⁻³ or more
Many orders of magnitude smaller than a metal
Poorly, but better as it warms

items: In a semiconductor, heating frees more carriers, so n rises and the material conducts better.
In an insulator nearly all the electrons are held in their atoms, so I = nAvq is almost zero even for a large potential difference.
A conductor has a very large n, a semiconductor a much smaller n, an insulator almost none.
A semiconductor's n increases with temperature.

checks.q: A current of 0.80 A flows for 2.5 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes and the number of electrons this represents.
Show that the equation I = nAvq follows from the definition of current.
checks.a: In time Δt carriers in a length vΔt pass a point. That volume is AvΔt and holds nAvΔt carriers. The charge is nAvΔtq, and I = ΔQ/Δt = nAvq.

checks.q: A copper wire and a silicon rod of the same area carry the same current. Explain why the drift velocity is much larger in the silicon.
checks.a: From I = nAvq, v = I / nAq. Silicon has a far smaller number density of charge carriers n, so v must be far larger for the same current.

blocks.text: Three basic definitions sit alongside current. The next notes use them in full.

items: Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = ΔQ / Δt.
Potential difference is the work done per unit charge: V = W / Q.
Resistance is defined as R = V / I.

blocks.text: Use I = nqvA to explain the huge range of resistivities between materials.

items: In a metal, n is very large, so a small drift velocity gives a large current. The resistivity is low.
In a semiconductor, n is much smaller, so the same potential difference gives a much smaller current. The resistivity is much higher.
In an insulator, n is almost zero, so the current is tiny and the resistivity is enormous.
Resistivities run from about 10⁻⁸ Ω m for metals to more than 10¹⁰ Ω m for good insulators.
